title: The tree on the road (Avot 3:7)
hookLine: a hard saying warns against breaking off study to admire a tree; many teachers read it as: the tree is Torah too
tomorrow: how bad is it to forget what you learned?

cards: Mid-run, a sky goes pink and orange, and somebody stops dead on the path to take a photo. Harmless, surely. So why would a sage frown at someone admiring a tree?
Avot has the line, and it's one of the hardest in the book.
Rabbi Yaakov says: one who walks on the road reviewing his learning, and breaks off to say, how beautiful is this tree, how beautiful is this field, Scripture counts it as if he put his life at risk.

teach.b: That can't be it, and the proof is in the Talmud.
It gives a blessing for anyone who goes out in the spring month of Nisan and sees trees in blossom, thanking God, who left nothing lacking in His world and made good trees for people to enjoy.

teach.h: THE TREE OF THE FIELD IS MAN'S LIFE.
teach.b: Deuteronomy, protecting fruit trees even in a siege, says, "for the tree of the field is man's life." A tradition with a blessing for blossoms isn't telling anyone to ignore them. So what's wrong on that road?
Look at one word: he breaks off.

He stops studying in order to admire, as if the tree were out there and the Torah in here, and he has to choose. Some teachers read the warning exactly there: the mistake is splitting the world in two.

teach.h: NO LINE BETWEEN TREE AND GOD.
teach.b: The tree is Torah too, if you look at it as part of the learning. Say the blessing, and admiring becomes study. Other readers hear it more plainly, as a warning about distraction on a dangerous road.
Both readings keep the walker's attention whole.
The puzzle's answer, on the first reading, is lovely: the sage isn't frowning at the tree. He's frowning at the line drawn between the tree and God.

how: Jewish tradition has blessings for the beauty of the natural world, including one said in the spring month of Nisan on seeing fruit trees in blossom (birkat ha-ilanot).

o: a law about planting trees beside every road
Avot's saying about pausing study to admire a tree
a story about a tree that blocked a rabbi's path

games.q: trees in the tradition — tap the pairs.
p: breaking off study to admire a tree
the spring month of the blossom blessing

s: Jewish tradition has a blessing for seeing trees in bloom
the Talmud gives one for blossoming trees in the month of Nisan.
some teachers read it as a warning against splitting the tree off from the holy.
Deuteronomy protects fruit trees even during a siege
for the tree of the field is man's life.

games.q: a friend who loves hiking says religion makes you choose between holy books and the outdoors. what does the tree puzzle suggest?
o: the tree can be part of the learning, not a break from it.
you have to pick: study is holy, nature is a distraction.
nature is holier, so the books can wait for winter.
games.why: a tradition with a blessing for blossoms isn't against trees. on one reading, the warning is against breaking off, as if the tree were outside Torah.

practice: Find one living thing you can see from here: a tree out the window, a houseplant, a weed in a crack. Look at it the way you'd read a line, slowly, finding one detail you missed, a vein, a color, a bent stem.
Some Jews say a blessing on seeing a beautiful tree; if you pray, you can let that thanks rise now.

wordCard.voice: The tree on the road: Avot's hard saying about breaking off study to admire a tree, read by some teachers as a warning against splitting the world from the holy.

orig.note: Hebrew: how beautiful is this tree, Avot 3:7.

carryVoice: Your line: the tree is torah too. Look at it that way and the walk becomes study. See you on the road.
